newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: China defends rights record, blasts West.
newsitem.headline: China defends rights record, blasts West.

text.p: The head of China's delegation to the U.N. Human Rights Commission defended his country's record on Tuesday and accused the United States and Europe of targeting only developing states for scrutiny in the forum.
Wu Jianmin, China's ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva, also said that Beijing awaited a proposal on prison visits from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

A spokesman for the Swiss humanitarian agency -- which has never had access to political prisoners in China -- confirmed that it was in talks with Beijing about a joint working party of experts meeting soon to begin talks on ICRC visits to detainees.
"We will propose the working party meet, probably in May. They would prepare the ground for discussion of visits," ICRC spokesman Joerg Stoecklin told Reuters.
"We have never visited political detainees in China. We have no idea how many there are," he added.
China was singled out in the U.S. State Department's annual report on human rights for having effectively silenced public dissent in 1996 through jailings, intimidation or exile.
Wu, addressing a news briefing on the second day of the U.N. body's annual six-week meeting, called for dialogue and cooperation rather than confrontation.

The United States and European Union are expected to bring a resolution expressing concern over abuses in China, but it looks likely to be defeated for the seventh year in a row due to Third World support for China in the 61-member body, diplomats said.
"The Human Rights Commission is not a courtroom," Wu said.
"Some delegates from developed countries behave like judges...We believe in cooperation based on equal footing."
Wu said: "The target is developing countries. What we are seeing in the Human Rights Commission is selectivity."
"We should deal with abuses in a very equitable way. This is not the case," he added.

All 72 resolutions adopted since 1992 following the end of the Cold War have been directed against developing countries, while all 17 of its U.N. special rapporteurs (investigators) are assigned to investigate developing countries, according to Wu.
"We believe that dialogue and cooperation are the right way to promote human rights," he added, adding that no country's record on human rights was perfect.
Echoing remarks by Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, who said in Beijing last Friday that any attempt to censure China was doomed to fail, Wu said:
"By tabling a draft resolution against my country, the Western countries are seeking confrontation. But if they choose confrontation again, I believe they will be defeated again."
Through economic reforms, the number of poor in China had dropped to 60 million from 250 million in 1978, according to Wu. "We want the Chinese to live better. We are doing that."
Asked about Amnesty International's criticism of China, Wu replied: "I think they make a living out of defaming my country...They are such profoundly biased people."
"Their statements are not serious. What they care about is not human rights -- it may be their jobs."
Western diplomats said Wu, who took up his post in Geneva in January 1996, has much at stake personally at the Commission.
"Wu is under a lot of pressure. If he doesn't get the resolution off the tracks and stop it from being approved, he may get called home," said one Western diplomat.
